positions.text: Player and Griffiths independently operationalize a bounded version of Kaal’s decay mechanism. In their multi-agent trust models, sliding windows delete older interaction records that no longer represent current behavior, while forgetting factors continuously down-weight older interactions; their adaptive RaPTaR method then uses current-behavior estimates to improve future partner selection. This supports treating reputation evidence as perishable rather than permanent. It does not establish Kaal’s stronger claim that the value of the future never reaches zero for every incumbent, nor does it validate his standing-token, staking, or rights architecture.

Mapping review tier: independent substantive scholarly-growth qualification.
The retained source studies trust and reputation assessment in simulated multi-agent systems, not Kaal’s specific agentic-reputation substrate.
Its forgetting factors and sliding windows make reputation evidence temporally perishable, but the paper does not use Kaal’s standing-token, staking, pool, settlement, or legal-rights architecture.
The experiments test partner selection under changing behaviour; they do not directly prove that the value of the future can never reach zero for every incumbent.
RaPTaR is presented as an improvement over fixed-rate forgetting, so the qualification does not endorse a single global decay parameter.

source_provenance.sourceProposition: Player and Griffiths model reputation information as time-sensitive: sliding windows delete older interactions that no longer represent current behaviour, forgetting factors continuously down-weight older interactions, and their adaptive RaPTaR method uses current-behaviour estimates to select better future interaction partners.

sourceEvidencePassages.text: A sliding window of size n retains the most recent n experiences. The intuition is that the most recent n instances capture an agent’s current behaviour, and older interaction records which are no longer relevant are deleted.
A forgetting factor, also referred to as a longevity factor, forgets at a constant rate with all instances being retained and more recent interactions weighted higher.
RaPTaR aims to improve an agent’s ability to assess another agent’s behaviour, and thereby select better partners for interactions.
RaPTaR outperforms all sliding windows with various window sizes (ws) and forgetting factor values (λ), where the improvement varies between 2-5%.
